title: How to Train Your Mamba for Time Series Forecasting

problem.claim: The paper addresses the use of State Space Models for time-series forecasting.

gap.claim: Existing applications often treat SSMs as black boxes, while the mechanisms behind their effectiveness and common claims about efficiency and expressiveness remain unclear or insufficiently substantiated.

contributions.claim: Establishes a theoretical connection between SSMs and classical spectral transformations from signal processing.
Conducts ablation studies examining properties of different SSM configurations.
Provides theoretical insight and empirical guidance for future research on SSM-based approaches in time-series forecasting.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report conducting comprehensive ablation studies on different SSM configurations.

narrative_sequence.summary: SSMs are presented as a powerful framework for sequence modeling and as particularly suitable for time-series data.
Applications of SSMs in time-series forecasting commonly treat the models as black boxes.
The mechanisms underlying SSM effectiveness and claims about efficiency and expressiveness are described as unclear or insufficiently substantiated.
The paper connects SSMs with classical spectral transformations and studies SSM configurations through ablation experiments.
The stated goal is to provide theoretical insight and empirical guidance for future SSM-based forecasting research.

source_observation.claim: The paper links SSMs to classical spectral transformations and examines configuration properties through ablation studies.

interpretation.claim: Combining mechanistic analysis with controlled configuration comparisons may make sequence models more interpretable and easier to reason about.

application.claim: For time-series modeling, analyze model behavior through established signal-processing concepts and configuration-level ablations.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that this approach improves forecasting accuracy, efficiency, or expressiveness.

unknowns: Datasets, baselines, metrics, and quantitative results
